Gather round, little wigglers. Settle your tails and open those dark eyes. Old Thistle here's got a tale for you tonight — one about the Iron River and how we toads saved it without ever needing a king to bark orders.

The pond was smaller then, back when my grandfather grew legs. Upstream sat the Machine-Belly of the Fish-Kings. They called it a Mill, but anyone who'd seen the gears grinding could tell it was a beast hungry for life. The Iron River fed into our home waters, clean and sweet. But then the fish built a dam. And they added filters that choked the water thick and gray.

Our elders gathered at Night-Rock, where the moon hits flat. Some wanted to send ambassadors. Others said fight. A few just grumbled about getting old. Nobody told anyone what to do. That's the way we've always done things — each voice matters, and nobody carries more weight because of fancy titles.

Thistle? That was me. Younger, skinnier, but full of fire. I had an idea. Not a big hero idea — just a small one.

"Their Mill runs on rhythm," I croaked. "Those great brass wheels turn when the river pushes them. If the river stops flowing right... they stop turning."

A ripple went through us. An elder named Puddleton squinted. "How do we make water stop?"

"We don't stop it," I said. "We give it somewhere else to go."

That was when Froglet Moll stood up. She knew tunnels better than anyone. Said there were hollows beneath the bank, left by ancient badgers who'd long since rotted away. Wide enough for currents to slip through if someone dug just right.

So that's what we did. No captain shouting schedules. No overseer counting hours. Just toads showing up with stones in their mouths, digging mud with webbed feet, passing dirt along lines until piles formed where they mattered. Moll showed the way. Strong backs moved earth. The rest of us kept watch, sent warnings when Fish-Guards patrolled upstream. We traded what we had: strength for guidance, time for knowledge. All of it voluntary. None of it forced.

Weeks passed. The work was slow. Sometimes days would pass with nothing to show. Other times, twenty pairs of hands opened the same hole until the whole thing bloomed open overnight.

Then came Dry Season.

The dam held firm. The filters clogged anyway. The Iron River backed up behind it, stagnant and warm. Our new channels carried the fresh flow around the bottleneck entirely. Clean water hit our end first. The Machine-Belly sputtered. Those great brass wheels ground to halt. The fish didn't starve or suffer — they just figured out better ways to live downstream once their mill stopped choking everything.

We never took anything that wasn't ours to take. Never hurt a single fish. We worked the land and found balance again, all of us contributing what we could until the job was done.

Here's the lesson, little ones: power isn't something you grab. It's something you grow together. When every toad decides what needs doing and does it without being ordered around, that decision sticks stronger than any chain. We won that day because no single throat could have sung loud enough to beat the mill. But hundreds of us? Working side-by-side, trusting each other to pull our weight? That changed everything.

Your ancestors weren't waiting for permission to build freedom. They built it one shovel-full at a time, and they're waiting to see what you'll add next.

Now swim. The pond doesn't defend itself.
